title: Gunnison Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gunnison wells have a 42 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $8,700-$16,200.
h1: What Gunnison Well Records Show Buyers
intro_html:
For properties within 5 miles of Gunnison, Colorado, DWR records show 2,702 permitted wells. Of those, 1,643 report a total depth, 507 report a pump yield, and 120 report a static water level. The local pattern is unusual for a mountain setting: many wells are shallow, but fractured-bedrock conditions can still make an individual site unpredictable.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and the records show strong reported yields where a pump test is available. That does not guarantee the same result on an untested lot. Before buying or building, review nearby well permits, confirm the intended use, and budget for access, casing, grout, pumping equipment, trenching, and electrical work.

sections.heading: Gunnison well depth: shallow records with mountain-bedrock uncertainty
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Gunnison is 42 feet. The middle half of reported wells falls between 27 and 83 feet, and 77% are under 100 feet. Another 17% are between 100 and 300 feet, while 5% fall between 300 and 600 feet and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 797 feet.

For a drilling bid, that spread matters more than the median alone. A shallow hole may be enough where groundwater is close to the surface, but fractured granite and gneiss can change conditions over a short distance. A contractor should review nearby completion records and discuss the possibility of extending the hole if the first target zone does not produce.

sections.heading: Reported Gunnison well yields are strong, but verify the test
sections.html:
Among the 507 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 76% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 22% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 3% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

Those results are encouraging for household use, but they are not a promise for a new well. Yield records cover only part of the mapped wells and may reflect different testing methods. Ask for the actual well construction and pump-test documents, not just a listing claim. Storage tanks can help manage demand when production is intermittent.

sections.heading: Gunnison water levels look stable across the reported decades
sections.html:
The median static water level is 8 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 5 and 18 feet. By measurement decade, the median was 9 feet in the 2000s, 8 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. That series does not show a clear dropping water table in these records.

Only 120 wells report a static water level, so the trend is limited rather than a site-specific guarantee. A water level can vary with season, pumping, recharge, and local geology. During due diligence, compare the subject parcel with nearby wells and ask whether a recent measurement was taken while the well was resting or under use.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Gunnison, and how old are the permits
sections.html:
Permit activity is concentrated in the late twentieth century and continues through the present. Records show 19 permits from the 1950s, 33 from the 1960s, 394 from the 1970s, 436 from the 1980s, 546 from the 1990s, 289 from the 2000s, 161 from the 2010s, and 157 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Bob Williams Drilling Co., listed as Williams, Robert F., appears most often with 1,121 records. Authorized, listed as Pe, Pg, appears on 114, and Peeples, Clyde L appears on 35. These records identify historical permit activity, not a recommendation or proof that a driller is available for a new project. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope, and references before signing.

sections.heading: What a Gunnison well may cost to drill and finish
sections.html:
Near Gunnison, the cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The typical drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 42-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,700 to $4,200. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $8,700 to $16,200.

These are planning figures, not a fixed bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, hard drilling, or a low-producing zone can change the total. Ask each contractor to separate drilling from completion equipment and site work. Also confirm what happens if the first hole is dry or produces less water than the intended home requires.

sections.heading: Mine sites, septic planning, and low-yield risks to check
sections.html:
Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 2,637 wells. Alluvial aquifers appear on 41 permits, and Dakota appears on 3. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells in the records. Mapped environmental sites within about 10 miles include 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 219 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites.

These mapped features do not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but they justify testing and a careful location review. Check water quality before closing and keep the well separated from septic components as required by the applicable rules. Confirm setbacks, driveway access, winter construction conditions, utility routes, and available buildable ground before relying on a well permit.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gunnison, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Gunnison is 42 feet. The middle half runs from 27 to 83 feet, and 77% are under 100 feet. Still, the deepest record is 797 feet, and fractured granite or gneiss can produce major differences between nearby parcels. Use neighboring completion records to plan a realistic drilling range.

faq.q: How much water do Gunnison wells produce?
faq.a: Among 507 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute, and 76% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful context, not a guarantee. Require a documented pump test for the specific well before assuming it can serve a home.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Gunnison?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the 42-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,700 to $4,200. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $8,700 to $16,200. A deeper hole, difficult access, or added completion work can raise the bid.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Gunnison, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Records show 11 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 219 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not prove a parcel is affected. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review nearby land uses, and test again after construction or repairs.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping around Gunnison?
faq.a: The available records do not show a clear decline. Median static water level was 9 feet below surface in the 2000s, 8 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. Only 120 wells report static water levels, so this is a broad indication rather than a guarantee for a specific parcel. Recent site measurements still matter.
